chapter: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
title: Rehearsing with Art Tatum and his harmonic ideas
summary: What he learned from Tatum: richer progressions, such as his Night and Day changes and his dissatisfaction with the bridge.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: We were talking about influences and things the last time, and I reread Beneath the Underdog, which I borrowed last Sunday, and it seemed to me that that period that you spent with Tatum rehearsing for a couple of months, whatever it was, must have been very -- for a kid, for a young bass player, a young musician, to have the opportunity to literally study with Tatum, must have really been very satisfying. And I wonder if you could say something about what you learned about that. How you felt about it.
I think I mentioned that last time.
You just said you had studied with him but -- rehearsed with him.
It's for how great he was, right?
(Unintelligible) what anybody did to help me.
I didn't mean to help you, necessarily. But it must have been --
I learned how to play his music.
I found that a song might appear to be one way, as far as progressions are concerned, chord changes, Art Tatum would find another way that was more beautiful and more complicated.
Like Night and Day, in the key of D.

I think the change would be a B Major 7. (inaudible), He used a F to a B flat seven, to a E flat seven to a D. On Night and Day." I wondered where it came from, I just wondered what made him think of things like that. He was never satisfied with the bridge, I remember that, him saying he wanted to fix the bridge.

Because he had such a great harmonic ear. And you have a great harmonic ear. I mean, one of the things that most people say about you is that Charles' harmonies are gorgeous. I just wondered how much of that was inspired by that period with Tatum.
